newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak FinMin blasts c.bank monetary policy-paper.
newsitem.headline: Slovak FinMin blasts c.bank monetary policy-paper.

text.p: Slovak Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik on Saturday criticised the restrictive monetary policy of the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS), saying it could have a negative impact on the entire economy.
"The attempts of the NBS to rapidly reduce growth in the money supply are inappropriate," Kozlik told the independent Bratislava daily Pravda.
Since the beginning of the year the NBS has introduced new measures to rein in a rapidly growing money supply and cool off a consumption-led boom.

The M2 key money supply aggregate rose around 19.0 percent year-on-year in November, compared with a 17.9 percent October rise. The 1996 M2 growth target was 11.6 percent and the central bank recently admitted the result is expected to above target.
"We have to ask whether the monetary policy has not missed its mark and is not negatively influencing the overall economic policy," Kozlik said.

The latest NBS move to hold securities repurchase tenders on a daily basis instead of quoting securities repo rates - which many domestic banks often used to refinance their activities - brought an acute liquidity shortage on the interbak market at the beginning of the year and pushed rates to around 27 percent.

"The situation on the interbank market, where interest rates are exceeding inflation by more than three times, was not caused by the government, but by the excessive restrictive monetary policy of the NBS," Kozlik said.

A fresh inflow of foreign funds, playing on the interest rate differential, helped ease rates to between 15.5 percent for overnight money and 17.5 percent for six-month funds over the last week in January.
The NBS has called for a more cautious approach to government development projects, saying that excessively expansive plans could hurt the stability of the currency.
The central bank has also warned that the ecomony is showing the first signs of overheating and that it would stick to the strict monetary policy to keep inflation under control.
The consumer price index rose 0.3 percent month-on-month in December, or 5.4 percent year-on-year.

The government plans to run a budget deficit of 36.9 billion crowns in 1997, up from last year's 25.5 billion. But the NBS said there could be problems refinancing the shortfall on the domestic market.
The cabinet is expected to issue some 70 billion crowns in state securities this year to cover the 1996 and 1997 deficits.
